The re-run of trail-review found 5 more issues. Three come from this round’s rework, and they show the pattern: each fix to how Entire places its own trailer opens a new edge case in another git mode.

What the re-run found
#	Finding	Real?	Caused by
A	--amend --no-edit on a #42 fix login commit: the restored trailer lands above the subject. The amend loses its link, and with --no-verify the trailer becomes the subject.	Yes	52ae5ec22 (restore moved above comments)
B	-m x -e -v with auto: the new selection rule counts git’s own # block, picks ;, appends the trailer below the diff, and git drops it.	Yes	this round’s fix 3
C	Plain -m messages ending in # lines get restructured: -m $'Fix login\n#123' loses #123 from its subject paragraph, and Fixes:\n#123 is split.	Yes	this round’s fix 1
D	The stamp marker isn’t recorded when prepare keeps a trailer (amend) or on the fast path, so those can still leave a dangling trailer.	Yes	gap in fix 2
E	Read-only explain, the export, and the review re-run guard still take the first ID anywhere. They can disagree with --generate and attach.	Yes	Main behaves the same; the branch made --generate diverge
F	A stamped ID left in the body is condensed by post-commit, but attach and explain --generate still see the commit as unlinked. commit-msg could move the trailer back into the final block.	Yes	design limit of fix 2
My recommendation: stabilize, then stop iterating

A, B and C share one root cause, and it has a small, principled fix. Git always writes a blank line before its comment block, so the block is “the trailing comment run with a blank line above it” (or the scissors line). Detecting the block from the message itself also tells auto whether there is a block to read back from, instead of guessing from the source word. Specifically:

A: a message made only of # lines has no block, so the trailer is appended.
B: the -m -e block is found, so the prefix is read from it.
C: Fix login\n#123 has no blank line above #123, so it isn’t treated as git’s block.

D is two more marker writes, one on the keep path and one on the fast path.

I’d defer E and F:

E: this changes read-only paths that behave as on main. It fits the squash follow-up, since squash commits are where several IDs appear.
F: it would add trailer relocation to commit-msg, which is a new mechanism with new edge cases.
What they cost meanwhile: a commit whose user moves the stamped trailer into the body is still condensed (by the marker), but attach and explain --generate treat it as unlinked. That would go under Known gap.

After that, one more local trail-review run, then stop. These rounds are now finding rare shapes: --no-edit plus all-comment subjects, -e -v plus auto, -m with # lines. Each fix in this area has produced a new one.

The fixes from this round are in a local placeholder commit (e941ea890) and not pushed. mise run check passed apart from load timeouts that pass when run alone.

# Branch review: `fix-checkpoint-trailer-block`

**Verdict: request changes**

Scope: `main...fix-checkpoint-trailer-block` at `2d16b3666`, covering one commit and seven changed files.

## Author intent

The change separates two meanings that the old checkpoint parser conflated:

- Whole-message parsing remains available for historical discovery, especially GitHub and native Git squash commits containing several embedded checkpoint trailers.
- Final-trailer-block parsing authorizes checkpoint creation, reuse, and mutation.

That split is the right design. The hook and attach changes apply it in several important places without breaking the existing squash-resume tests. The implementation is not complete, however: two mutation paths still trust whole-message results, and the strict parser does not match Git's trailer grammar.

No pull request currently exists for this branch. The related [PR #2168](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2168) remains open.

## Spec

### Act on

#### High: `checkpoint explain --commit ... --generate` can write to a body-selected checkpoint

[`runExplainAuto`](cmd/entire/cli/explain.go#L617) and [`runExplainCommit`](cmd/entire/cli/explain.go#L2994) still resolve commit linkage with whole-message `ParseCheckpoint`. When `--generate` is present, that ID reaches [`store.Write`](cmd/entire/cli/explain.go#L1095).

A commit body can therefore name an existing but unrelated checkpoint and cause:

```text
commit body
    -> ParseCheckpoint(existing ID)
    -> checkpoint explain --generate --force
    -> generateCheckpointSummary
    -> store.Write(existing ID)
```

This violates the recorded requirement to "prevent untrusted checkpoint-shaped commit-body text from being accepted in unsafe contexts."

Use final-block parsing when commit resolution leads to summary generation. Keep whole-message parsing only for read-only discovery. Add regressions for both explicit `--commit` and positional commit fallback.

#### Medium: legacy migration still lets body text authorize reconciliation

[`migrateShadowBranchIfNeeded`](cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_migration.go#L72) scans the whole message when a legacy state lacks `LastCheckpointCommitHash`. A matching body ID advances both `BaseCommit` and `AttributionBaseCommit`, skipping normal migration and changing future attribution.

This conflicts with the intended boundary that body IDs are discovery candidates while final-block IDs authorize mutation.

Require final-block evidence for the legacy fallback, or decline reconciliation when the recorded commit hash is unavailable. Add a legacy-state regression with a matching body ID followed by a different final trailer block.

### Consider

None.

### Noted

The existing squash-history semantics are preserved. All three named squash-resume unit tests passed unchanged.

### Dismissed

None.

**Worst spec issue:** `--generate` can persist a summary to a checkpoint selected solely by commit-body text.

## Standards

### Act on

#### High: leading whitespace turns body text into an authorizing trailer

[`ParseAllCheckpointsFromFinalTrailerBlock`](cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go#L162) and [`finalTrailerBlock`](cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go#L306) left-trim lines before classifying and parsing them.

This line is therefore accepted:

```text
  Entire-Checkpoint: a1b2c3d4e5f6
```

Git 2.50's `git interpret-trailers --parse` returns no trailer for the same message. The branch parser nevertheless lets that line choose the ID used by PostCommit condensation and attach.

Do not remove leading spaces or tabs when validating final-block trailer lines. Add production-path regressions for PostCommit and attach, not only parser tests.

#### Medium: commit-message comment handling does not follow Git configuration

[`parseCheckpointFromCommitMessageFile`](cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go#L290) strips only `#` suffix lines. Git permits a configurable `core.commentChar`, and default cleanup preserves comment-prefixed lines when no editor runs. See the official [`git commit` cleanup documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit/2.52.0).

This creates two failure shapes:

- A repository using another comment character can hide a legitimate final trailer behind Git's comment block.
- A `git commit -m` or `-F` message can contain real `#` user content that this helper discards before deciding an earlier checkpoint-shaped body line is final.

Resolve Git's effective comment character or apply Git-equivalent cleanup rules. Cover editor, `-m`/`-F`, and custom-comment-character flows.

### Consider

#### Support Git trailer continuations

[`finalTrailerBlock`](cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go#L317) walks backward only while every line independently matches `Key: value`. Git accepts continuation lines beginning with whitespace, so a multiline trailer after `Entire-Checkpoint` can make the branch parser reject the entire block even though Git accepts it.

This may produce a duplicate checkpoint ID during prepare/amend or make PostCommit skip condensation. Either support continuation lines or explicitly document and test the narrower grammar.

#### Exercise attach through its durable boundary

`TestAttachIgnoresCheckpointShapedBodyText` calls `resolveCheckpointID` and `promptAmendCommit` separately. It does not prove through `runAttach` that a forged checkpoint remains unmodified and a fresh checkpoint receives the attached session.

A full-path regression should inspect the persistent store after attach.

### Noted

- The strict maintainability pass found no structural regression. The large hook file was already over 1,000 lines; this change did not cross that threshold or scatter the core parser policy.
- The parser change adds no lock or interruption point. Parser selection occurs before existing writes, so cleanup and recovery semantics are otherwise unchanged.
- Median `PrepareCommitMsg` time was 15.20 ms on this branch versus 15.13 ms on `main`, a difference of roughly 0.5% and within sample noise.

### Dismissed

One adversarial reviewer flagged `hasUserContent` for treating every checkpoint-shaped line as Entire metadata. That behavior predates this branch and requires a commit whose only user content is itself checkpoint-shaped. It is not a regression introduced here.

**Worst standards issue:** the strict parser accepts a Git-invalid indented body line as mutation authority.

## Correctness model

### Who owns each write?

- PrepareCommitMsg chooses the checkpoint ID; PostCommit owns condensation into persistent checkpoint storage.
- Attach chooses or reuses an ID, writes the attached session, then best-effort amends the commit.
- `checkpoint explain --generate` owns summary persistence.
- Session migration owns `BaseCommit` and `AttributionBaseCommit` reconciliation.

The first two owners now use the strict parser in their main paths. Summary generation and legacy migration do not.

### What happens around interruption?

The diff changes classification before existing writes. It does not add a lock, subprocess, temporary file, or new partial-write state. Existing write and recovery owners remain responsible before and after the decision. The outstanding risk is wrong-target mutation, not new interruption behavior.

### Which tests observe the real contract?

- The PrepareCommitMsg regression enters the production hook and would fail on the old code.
- The attach test observes helpers rather than the durable store contract.
- No regression covers body-selected summary generation, legacy migration, indented pseudo-trailers, custom Git comment characters, or trailer continuation lines.

## Multi-model agreement

Three independent reviewers examined the same intent and diff:

| Finding | Agreement | Disposition |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Explain generation trusts body IDs | 3/3 | Act on |
| Indented pseudo-trailer accepted | 2/3 | Act on |
| Legacy migration trusts body IDs | 2/3 | Act on |
| Git comment handling is hard-coded | 1/3 | Act on after local verification |
| `hasUserContent` removes body-shaped lines | 1/3 | Dismissed as pre-existing |

A commit whose every staged path is held gets no fresh trailer; otherwise session matching sees only the redo's other staged paths (`redo.others`, the same rename-free view). # General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier, changes which command to run, or adds a new place that reports an existing failure, check every place that already reports it (status, doctor, enable, help text) so they all give the same fix. Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one, or one command prints the same failure twice with different fixes.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
- When decoding user-editable JSON into maps or pointers, skip null elements before writing to them; `[null]` decodes to a nil map and a write panics.
- Review a PR that is behind main against current main, not its own base: build both and run the same repro. Its tests pass on its old base even when keeping its side of a conflict would undo a fix merged since.
- When wiring user config into a new path, test it with a broken config too. A user rule that silently fails to load leaks the same way as one that was never wired.
- Make a fail-closed check fire only on the failure it guards against, not on a whole class of errors. A refusal on any settings error blocks unrelated cases and pushes users toward a less safe escape hatch, such as an unredacted `--raw` bundle.

content.text:
Review target: `origin/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block..HEAD`

`xhigh effort → 10 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → sweep → ≤15 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at extra-high effort: catch every real bug. At
this level, catching real bugs matters more than avoiding false positives — a
missed bug ships. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (5 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 8 each)

Run **10 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 8 candidate findings**. Do NOT let one angle's conclusions
suppress another's — if two angles flag the same line for different reasons,
record both.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Angle D — language-pitfall specialist

Scan for the classic pitfalls of the diff's language/framework — for example:
JS falsy-zero, `==` coercion, closure-captured loop var; Python mutable default
args, late-binding closures; Go nil-map write, range-var capture; SQL injection;
timezone/DST drift; float equality. Flag any instance the diff introduces.

### Angle E — wrapper/proxy correctness

When the PR adds or modifies a type that wraps another (cache, proxy, decorator,
adapter): check that every method routes to the wrapped instance and not back
through a registry/session/global — e.g. a caching provider holding a
`delegate` field that resolves IDs via `session.get(...)` instead of
`delegate.get(...)` will re-enter the cache or recurse. Also check that the
wrapper forwards all the methods the callers actually use.

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity. Do NOT drop on uncertainty.

## Phase 3 — Sweep for gaps

Take one more pass (same context — no subagent) as a fresh reviewer who has the deduplicated list. Re-read
the diff and enclosing functions looking ONLY for defects not already listed.
Do not re-derive or re-confirm anything already there — the job is gaps. Focus
on what the first pass tends to miss: moved/extracted code that dropped a guard
or anchor; second-tier footguns (dataclass default evaluated once, `hash()`
non-determinism, lock-scope shrink, predicate methods with side effects);

content.text:
**Brief: what `origin/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block..HEAD` does** (the WIP round plus this session's round)

- **For users:** Entire's commit hooks now write the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer where git will record it in every common `git commit` mode, so it lands in the final trailer block and links the commit. The modes are `-m`, `-m -e`, the editor, `-v`, `--amend`, `--amend --no-edit`, `-C`, templates, and `core.commentChar`/`auto`/`commit.cleanup` configs. The user's own lines stay where they typed them. The per-commit read-only views (`explain <commit>`, `explain --commit`, the export, and the review re-run guard) now show the same checkpoint that `--generate` and attach write.
- **Why:** this PR's security rule (only the final trailer block authorizes checkpoint writes) made trailer placement a correctness requirement. Every mode that left the trailer outside the final block lost its link. Readers that still took the first ID anywhere disagreed with the writers.
- **How:**
  - `GIT_EDITOR=:` (githooks(5)) tells both hooks whether git opens the editor.
  - Git's comment block is the trailing comment run after a blank line, or the scissors line.
  - The `auto` prefix is read back from that block, with a consistency check.
  - The stamp marker is recorded on every path where prepare leaves a link.
  - A per-hook snapshot means one `git config` read per prepare.
  - `strategy.CommitCheckpoint` is the one read-only resolver.
- **Performance:** one `git config` spawn fewer per squash or redo commit (measured: 8 → 7 on those tests). Read-only views add one spawn only when the final block names no ID but the message mentions one.
- **Compatibility:**
  - Messages git doesn't open now always get the trailer appended, so the layout differs from the pushed branch.
  - Squash commits now show their last final-block checkpoint instead of the first.
  - It relies on git's `GIT_EDITOR` contract.
- **Uncertain:** whether any agent harness or CI exports `GIT_EDITOR=:` itself, which is indistinguishable from git's own signal.
- **Evidence:**
  - `entire search` found the earlier "Place inherited trailers above git's comment block" and "Keep redone trailers above git's comment block" commits.
  - `entire graph impact`: `EditorCommentBlockStart` has 3 direct and 16 transitive callers, and `addCheckpointTrailerAboveComments` has 9 direct callers. Both match what I reviewed.
  - I didn't run `entire why`/`blame`: the central lines are this session's own work, and their intent is above.
  - The librarian was unreachable (1Password signed out, HTTP 302), so there is no Linear or Slack context.

findings.failure_scenario: Shell or CI exports GIT_EDITOR=: and runs plain `git commit` with an empty message. Git still writes its block and strips comments. Prepare (edited=false) appends the trailer below the block with no explanation. commit-msg (edited=false, default cleanup keeps comments) finds the '# Please enter…' lines and keeps the trailer. Git records a commit whose whole message is `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>`. The pushed branch aborted here via the explanation marker. With -v the trailer also lands below the scissors line and is lost.

core.commentChar=auto, HEAD recorded as 'My change

Yes, a small real-git test is in scope, and I'd add it to this PR. The full matrix isn't, and I wouldn't split the PR.

**Why it's in scope.** The PR's central claim is "only the final trailer block links a commit, and Entire's own trailer always lands there." That rule is what made placement matter at all: on main, the reader scanned the whole message, so the trailer's position mostly didn't matter. A test showing the trailer really ends up in the final block under real `git commit` is the evidence for the PR's own claim, not new work. Simulated tests can't provide that evidence, because they share the code's assumptions about git.

**Why I wouldn't split.** The security core can't ship safely on its own. The writers on main weren't aware of the final block (amends appended after git's comment block, and `-m -e -v` put the trailer below the scissors line). With only the stricter reader, those commits would lose their links. The placement work is what makes the core safe to merge, so it belongs in the same PR.

```
fix(trailers): place and read the trailer as git records it

Only the final trailer block links a commit, so each git commit mode
that left Entire's trailer elsewhere lost its link. Prepare and
commit-msg guessed what git already knows, and some readers kept the old
rule:

- Git runs its commit hooks with GIT_EDITOR=: when it opens no editor
  (githooks(5)). Both hooks now read that instead of the source word or
  the message's last line: a -m, --amend --no-edit or -C message gets
  its trailer appended with its own lines in place, a -m -e one gets it
  above git's comment block, and commit-msg judges an emptied message by
  git's cleanup.
- Git's comment block is the run of comment lines after a blank line
  that ends the message, or the scissors line. core.commentChar=auto is
  read back from that block, else picked by git's own rule.
- Prepare reads the final block as post-commit does: cleaned with git's
  prefix, then read by the trailer grammar, where auto is "#". Under
  auto with a cleanup that keeps comments, the trailer goes after git's
  kept block instead.
- Post-commit accepts the trailer prepare left, stamped, restored or
  kept, wherever the user's edits moved it, through a per-worktree
  marker.
- explain <commit>, explain --commit, the export and the review re-run
  guard show the checkpoint --generate and attach use: the final block's
  last ID, falling back to the first ID anywhere only when it names
  none. --generate names the checkpoints it refuses for sitting outside
  the block.
- prepare-commit-msg reads git's comment config once per hook.

TestTrailerAuthority_RealGitCommits runs real git commit with the hooks
and a scripted editor across these modes.
```
